1065.title: Handed down (CCC 74–79)
1065.hook: the apostles handed on their mission to bishops
1065.howItsDone: At every Mass, the Eucharistic Prayer names the pope and the local bishop, and bishops are ordained by other bishops through the laying on of hands, which Catholics understand as the succession from the apostles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, revelation: God making himself known in stages, Noah, Abraham, Israel, then the Son. Your line was step by step. Today, how it's passed on.

"And the things which thou hast heard of me by many witnesses, the same commend to faithful men, who shall be fit to teach others also." That's Paul, writing to Timothy, in the Douay-Rheims. Follow the people in that one sentence. Paul speaks. Timothy hears. Timothy hands it to faithful men. They teach others. And the others, presumably, will teach others again. It's a relay, written into a single verse. Today's word is that relay, as the Catholic Church understands it: apostolic succession.
screen: `PAUL TO TIMOTHY.` → `TO FAITHFUL MEN.` → `TO OTHERS ALSO.`

segments.voice: Day two hundred ninety-three paired scripture and Tradition; today follows the line further. The Catechism calls the handing-on of the faith tradition, a living transmission. The apostles, it says, handed on what they received in two ways: by word of mouth, in their preaching, example, and the communities and customs they set up; and in writing, in the books that became the New Testament. Then a third thing. To keep the gospel whole and alive in the Church, the apostles left bishops as their successors, handing over their own teaching role. That's apostolic succession. Catholic teaching sees today's bishops as successors of the apostles, each ordained by the laying on of hands by bishops before him. An early letter already speaks this way. A letter from the church in Rome to the church in Corinth, which tradition credits to Clement, says the apostles appointed leaders and made provision that, when those leaders died, other approved men should succeed to their ministry. Orthodox Christians also hold to the succession of bishops. Other churches understand faithfulness to the apostles in other ways, some by holding to the apostles' teaching in scripture rather than to a line of bishops. And Catholic teaching adds a limit: the Church's teaching office is not above the word of God, but serves it. The bishop is a link in the chain, not the source of what runs through it. In the Catholic picture, it's less a family tree of power than a chain of hands, each passing on what it was given, and answerable for passing it on whole.

segments.voice: Think of your bishop, by name if you know it, or simply whoever holds that role where you live, and the weight of the job: one person asked to keep an old message whole, in a place full of new problems. If you pray, say their name and ask God's help for them; if you don't, wish them wisdom plainly, the way you'd wish it for anyone carrying something heavy.
Apostolic succession. The bishops as successors of the apostles, a teaching role handed on hand to hand, in service of the word of God. Today's word.
Your line: an unbroken line. Paul to Timothy, Timothy to faithful men, and on to others also. Until tomorrow.

1066.title: The four senses of scripture (CCC 115–119)
1066.hook: literal, allegorical, moral and anagogical: one text, many depths
1066.howItsDone: Catholic preachers and readers draw on the four senses when they explain scripture, and the Church's liturgy often pairs an Old Testament story with a Gospel reading so that one sheds light on the other.

segments.voice: Yesterday, apostolic succession: a teaching handed on, hand to hand. Your line was an unbroken line. Today, how the Church reads what was handed on.

On a piano stand, a sheet of music lies open. A beginner reads the notes, one at a time, and gets them right. A teacher, reading the same page, hears the harmony moving underneath. The composer sees where the whole piece is heading, pages ahead. Nobody has changed a single note; the depth of the reading changed. The Catholic tradition reads scripture a little like that: the same verse, read on several levels at once. Today's word: the four senses.
screen: `THE BEGINNER READS THE NOTES.` → `THE TEACHER HEARS THE HARMONY.` → `SAME PAGE, DEEPER READING.`

segments.voice: The Catechism names two senses of scripture, the literal and the spiritual, then divides the spiritual into three. Four in all: literal, allegorical, moral, anagogical. Underneath everything, the literal: what the words actually say, what the writer meant. Following Thomas Aquinas, the Catechism says every other sense is built on this one. Then the allegorical: how events point to Christ. Paul uses the very word. Writing about Abraham's two sons in Galatians, he says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Which things are said by an allegory." Then the moral: what the text asks of how we live. Paul again, about Israel in the desert: these things "are written for our correction." Then the anagogical: where it all leads in the end, toward the life of heaven. The Catechism's own example of the allegorical sense is the crossing of the Red Sea, a sign of Christ's victory and of Christian baptism. Some readers run that story through all four. Literally, Israel walks through the sea and out of slavery. Allegorically, Christ's victory, and baptism. Morally, leaving behind what holds a person captive. Anagogically, the last crossing, into the promised land. The Catechism also quotes a medieval rhyme that packs it into a pocket: the letter teaches what happened; allegory, what to believe; the moral sense, what to do; anagogy, where you're heading. It isn't a secret code. The literal comes first, and the other senses grow out of it, not away from it. The page stays the same. The reading goes deeper.
screen: `LITERAL FIRST, UNDER EVERYTHING.` · `ALLEGORICAL, MORAL, ANAGOGICAL.` · `THE RED SEA, FOUR WAYS.` · `WHAT HAPPENED, BELIEVE, DO, HEADING.`

segments.voice: Say this line from the Psalms slowly, in the Douay-Rheims: "I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord." Then ask four questions, a breath between each: what happened, pilgrims setting off for the temple in Jerusalem; what might it show about Christ; what does it ask of me today; and where is it heading, in the end? Some may stay unanswered, and that's fine; if you pray, say the line again as your own.

1067.title: I believe, we believe (CCC 166–167)
1067.hook: faith is personal but never solitary
1067.howItsDone: At baptism, the parents and godparents of a child, or the adult being baptized, profess the faith by answering the priest's questions; at Sunday Mass the congregation stands and says the Creed together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four senses: literal, allegorical, moral, anagogical. Your line was one text, four depths. Today, the first words of the Creed.

A Sunday afternoon baptism. The baby is asleep, or furious. The priest turns to the parents and godparents and asks, one question at a time, whether they believe in God, the Father almighty, and in his Son, and in the Holy Spirit. Each time they answer out loud: I do. The next Sunday, at an ordinary Mass, the whole church stands and says the Creed together, every voice at once. Same faith. One time it sounds like a single voice; the next, like a crowd. Today: I believe, we believe.
screen: `A BAPTISM: I DO.` → `A SUNDAY MASS: EVERY VOICE AT ONCE.` → `I BELIEVE, WE BELIEVE.`

segments.voice: Day one hundred one took the Apostles' Creed line by line; today, just its first words. The Catechism notices the grammar. I believe is the faith of the Church professed by each believer personally, above all at baptism; that's how the Apostles' Creed speaks. We believe is the faith confessed by the bishops gathered in council, or by the whole assembly at worship; that's how the creed of the councils speaks. Both are true at once. Faith, the Catechism says, is a personal act: a person's free response to God who reveals himself. But it's never an isolated act. No one can believe alone, it says, just as no one can live alone. Nobody gave themselves faith, any more than they gave themselves life. It was received from others, and it's meant to be handed on. A moment in Mark's Gospel holds both sides. A father brings his son, who is suffering terribly, to Jesus. Jesus speaks of believing, and the father cries out, in the Douay-Rheims, "I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief." It's as personal as a sentence can be, and he says it in a crowd, on someone else's behalf, for his child. The Catechism recalls the baptism rite of the Roman Ritual, where the minister asks what is being sought from God's Church, and the answer is one word: faith. The Church, it says, believes first, and carries each believer. Even a private prayer, in the Catholic picture, is said inside a very large we.

segments.voice: If you can, say the Creed with someone, at Mass, at home, or quietly along with a recording. If you're on your own, say or think the first two words, I believe, and let faces come to mind: the people whose faith reached you somehow, a grandparent, a teacher, a friend, a stranger in a pew. If you pray, thank God for them by name; if you don't, think of who carried what you know, in any part of life.

1068.title: The Creed's shape (CCC 190)
1068.hook: three parts: Father and creation, Son and redemption, Spirit and sanctification
1068.howItsDone: Catholics profess the Creed at Sunday Mass and at baptism, and the Catechism's first part is laid out in the Creed's order, beginning with the Father and creation, then the Son, then the Holy Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, I believe, we believe: faith that's personal and never solitary. Your line was no one believes alone. Today, the shape of what's believed.

Break a seal in two. Keep one half, and give the other to a friend who's leaving for somewhere far away. Years later, a stranger knocks at your door and holds out a jagged piece. You take out yours and put the edges together. If they fit, you know who sent this person. In Greek, a token like that was called a symbolon. The Catechism says it's an old name for the Creed: a sign by which believers recognize each other. Today, the shape of that piece.
screen: `A SEAL BROKEN IN TWO.` → `DO THE EDGES FIT?` → `THE CREED AS A SYMBOLON.`

segments.voice: Day two hundred ninety-seven met the Trinity; today, how it shapes the Creed. The Catechism points to baptism. Jesus sends the apostles out, in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Going therefore, teach ye all nations; baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Because the faith is first professed at baptism, the Creed is built around those same three names. So it falls into three parts: the Father and the work of creation; the Son and the mystery of redemption; the Holy Spirit, the source of our sanctification, the making holy of people. The Catechism borrows that division from an older one, the Roman Catechism, which followed the same plan. Three things to notice. First, it's a story as much as a list: from the making of all things, to the rescue of what went wrong, to the slow work of making people holy, ending with eternal life. Second, three parts don't mean three gods. The Creed confesses one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and Catholic teaching holds that all three are at work in every part; the division says which work is chiefly spoken of where. Third, the shape is useful. If you lose your place in the Creed, the turns are easy to find: one where it comes to Jesus Christ, the Son, and one where it comes to the Holy Spirit. One God, making, saving and making holy.
screen: `IN THE NAME OF FATHER, SON, SPIRIT.` · `FATHER: CREATION.` · `SON: REDEMPTION. SPIRIT: SANCTIFICATION.` · `ONE GOD, NOT THREE.`

segments.voice: If you have the Creed in a missal, a prayer book or on your phone, read it slowly and mark the two places it turns: to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. If not, walk the three movements on the breath: something made, the world or your own body; then something mended; then something slowly growing better, and around again. If you pray, you can name each movement to God.
The Creed's shape. Three parts: the Father and creation, the Son and redemption, the Spirit and sanctification, all one God. Today's word.
Your line: three movements. Made, mended, and made holy, by one God. Rest well.

1069.title: Almighty (CCC 268–278)
1069.hook: God shows his almighty power most of all in mercy
1069.howItsDone: Catholics profess God as the Father almighty in the Creed at Mass, and some of the Church's prayers, including the one the Catechism quotes, address God's power and his mercy together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Creed's shape: Father, Son and Spirit. Your line was three movements. Today, one word from the Creed's first line.

What does strength look like? A weightlifter with the bar overhead. A storm that peels a roof off. A fist on a table. Now another scene: a big man down on one knee on a sidewalk, tying a toddler's shoe, careful not to pull the laces too tight. That's strength too, the kind that holds itself back. The Creed calls God the Father almighty, and when the Catechism explains that word, it makes a claim about where that power shows most. Today's word: almighty.
screen: `A WEIGHTLIFTER. A STORM. A FIST.` → `A MAN TYING A TODDLER'S SHOE.` → `WHERE DOES POWER SHOW MOST?`

segments.voice: Almighty means able to do all things. Mary sings it in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "he that is mighty, hath done great things to me." But the Book of Wisdom ties that power to something unexpected, saying to God: "thou hast mercy upon all, because thou canst do all things." Mercy because of power, not in spite of it. The Catechism pairs the Creed's two words, Father and almighty, and says they shed light on each other: a father's power, never arbitrary, never a whim. Then it faces the hard question that day two hundred ninety-nine called why evil. If God is almighty, why so much suffering? The Catechism admits that faith in God's power can be put to the test by evil. Its answer points to the cross, where God looks weakest; Paul calls the crucified Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. The Catechism says God shows his almighty power by turning people from their sins and bringing them back to friendship with him. And it quotes a prayer of the Roman Mass that goes further: God shows his almighty power most of all by sparing and by showing mercy. On this reading, any force can break things; it takes a deeper power to forgive, and to heal what's broken. The Creed's first adjective isn't a threat hanging over the world. It's the strength of someone who can afford to be gentle.

segments.voice: Think of a moment coming up today when you'll hold a little power: over a child, a coworker who made a mistake, someone on a customer service line, a slow driver ahead of you. Picture it clearly, then picture using that power gently, a softer word, a little patience, a small offense let go, and rehearse it once, start to finish. If you pray, ask God for that kind of strength; if you don't, just hold the picture steady.

1070.title: Providence (CCC 302–308)
1070.hook: God guides creation, and invites us to cooperate
1070.howItsDone: Catholics speak of trusting in divine providence, and pair that trust with work; some pray before a task or a decision and offer the day's work to God in a morning prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, almighty: a power the Catechism says shows most in mercy. Your line was power as mercy. Today, how that power guides.

"Behold the birds of the air, for they neither sow, nor do they reap, nor gather into barns: and your heavenly Father feedeth them." Jesus says it on a hillside, in the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims. It's a lovely line. It also raises a fair question from anyone with a job and a rent payment due on the first. So should we stop sowing? Today's word is the Catechism's way of fitting God's care and our work together: providence.
screen: `THE BIRDS NEITHER SOW NOR REAP.` → `A RENT PAYMENT DUE.` → `SHOULD WE STOP SOWING?`

segments.voice: Day three hundred sixty-six met providence in Joseph's story; today, the Catechism's account. It starts somewhere surprising. Creation wasn't made finished. It was made on a journey, heading toward a fullness it hasn't reached yet, and providence is the name for the ways God guides it along that road. Scripture, the Catechism says, shows that care as concrete and close, reaching the smallest things. That's why Jesus asks for a child's kind of trust: "Seek ye therefore first the kingdom of God, and his justice, and all these things shall be added unto you." Then the turn. In the Catholic picture, God isn't a puppeteer. He gives his creatures not only existence but the dignity of acting on their own, of being real causes for each other. And to human beings he gives the power to share in providence freely: to tend the earth, to work, to look after one another. Writing about himself and the others who labored with him in Corinth, Paul says, in the Douay-Rheims, "we are God's coadjutors." Helpers, fellow workers. The Catechism takes up that phrase for people more broadly: through their actions, their prayers, and even their sufferings, people can enter freely into God's plan, and so become God's fellow workers. So, back to the birds. They don't sow. People do, and on this reading, the sowing itself can be part of how God provides. Providence isn't a reason to sit still, and it isn't a promise that nothing will go wrong. It's trust that God is at work, and an invitation to work alongside.

1071.title: Visible and invisible (CCC 325–327)
1071.hook: heaven and earth, angels and all that is
1071.howItsDone: At Sunday Mass Catholics profess God as maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible, and the Church keeps feasts for the angels in its calendar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, providence: God guiding a creation still on its way. Your line was we are co-workers. Today, everything that is, seen and unseen.

Take stock of the last minute. Air you can't see went in and out of your lungs. A signal nobody can see probably carried these words to wherever you are. Somewhere, someone's trust in you, which you can't see either, is part of why your day holds together. A lot of what holds a life up is invisible. The Creed said at Sunday Mass calls God the maker of all things visible and invisible. Today we stay with that phrase.
screen: `AIR YOU CAN'T SEE.` → `TRUST YOU CAN'T SEE.` → `ALL THINGS VISIBLE AND INVISIBLE.`

segments.voice: Start with the bigger phrase, heaven and earth. In scripture, the Catechism says, it means all that exists: creation as a whole. The earth is the world of people. Heaven can mean the sky, or God's own place, our Father who art in heaven, or the place of the angels around God. Then the Creed adds: visible and invisible. Paul says it in Colossians, in the Douay-Rheims: "in him were all things created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible." A Church council, quoted in the Catechism, put it plainly: from the beginning God made both orders of creation, the spiritual and the bodily, the angelic and the earthly, and then the human, made of both together. In the Catholic picture, people stand where the two orders meet: a body, like everything on earth, and a spirit. That's tomorrow, body and soul. Invisible here doesn't mean imaginary. It means real things eyes can't catch, like the angels and the human soul. The Creed holds that all of creation, seen and unseen, is made by God, and nothing created sits outside that making. Look back over this week: the faith handed down, scripture at four depths, I believe inside we believe, the Creed's three movements, power as mercy, providence and its co-workers, and now the maker of all things. In the Creed's one short phrase, the seen and the unseen stand side by side, on the same list of things made.
screen: `HEAVEN AND EARTH: ALL THAT EXISTS.` · `VISIBLE AND INVISIBLE, IN COLOSSIANS.` · `TWO ORDERS, AND HUMANS MADE OF BOTH.` · `INVISIBLE DOESN'T MEAN IMAGINARY.`

segments.voice: Feel the air coming in, cool, then going out, warm; you've never seen it. Now name one more invisible thing your life leans on, someone's loyalty, a promise kept, your own memory, a love you've been given, and let it be as real as the chair under you. If you pray, thank God, maker of things seen and unseen, for it; if you don't, simply let your attention rest there.
